items.t: Rheinmetall's Dortmund Exit Is a Footnote; the Real Story Is Whether Its Growth Can Be Booked on Tim
sum: Rheinmetall and Borussia Dortmund confirmed yesterday that their sponsorship arrangement will lapse when the current contract expires on 30 June 2027. The decision was mutual, and the defence group will keep its stadium box among other ties, so the relationship winds down by agreement rather than rupture. No financial read-across is available from the move.

For anyone holding the stock, the more pressing question sits elsewhere: how much weight should public visibility carry when a company has to make good on its operating promises? At Rheinmetall, execution now commands more attention than exposure — a shift with a concrete trigger in the numbers.

On 5 November the company reported revenue of €8.4bn for the first nine months of 2026, with operating profit above €1.3bn. Those figures speak to the substance of the business. They only underpin the equity case, though, if Rheinmetall can reliably support expectations for the rest of the year — and that is precisely where last week's guidance cut bites.

Rheinmetall lowered its 2026 revenue forecast to around €13.2bn, citing delays on the Arminius project and on acceptance procedures for artillery ammunition. The tension is stark: revenue for the nine-month period grew 38%, while operating profit reached €1,339m, up 69%. Strong trading and a more cautious outlook can both be justified at once, and that combination is what makes the shares demanding.

Order intake for the same nine months came in at €19.1bn, a metric that belongs alongside revenue and earnings in any assessment of how the business is travelling. Between demand and booked business sit operational steps — nominations, deliveries, sign-offs — and delays dent a forecast even when the underlying project survives intact.

A fresh analyst note published today sharpens the same theme, flagging possible slippage or a scaling-back of the F127 frigate programme. According to media reports, the assessment kept a neutral rating and a €1,000 price target. A potential delay is a risk to be weighed, not a confirmed postponement.

A second note on Tuesday pointed to execution risks and hard-to-read demand, and raised the possibility that the 2030 revenue target could be trimmed at the capital markets day. That too is an expectation, not a company decision.

items.t: Rheinmetall's €900 Consensus: Two Brokers, One Target, and a Guidance Cut That Puts Execution Firs
sum: Акции Rheinmetall упали на 4,0% в среду, что продлило тяжелые времена для европейских оборонных компаний и стало новым напоминанием инвесторам о том, что изменение рейтинга сектора больше не является односторонней сделкой. Падение произошло, когда два брокера сошлись на одной и той же целевой цене в 900 евро в противоположных направлениях: один снизил оценку, другой полностью отказался от колла на покупку.

Более широкий фон был неумолим. По данным Handelsblatt, с середины января индекс обороны в индексе Stoxx Europe 600 упал на 17%. Rheinmetall также пришлось принять на себя давление со стороны конкретной компании: снижение целевых цен и растущие вопросы о том, сможет ли группа реализовать свой план роста.

Во вторник компания Berenberg понизила целевую цену Rheinmetall до 900 евро с 1020 евро, сохранив при этом рекомендацию «Держать». Аналитик Джордж МакВиртер указал на риск исполнения как на главную проблему и ожидает, что компания сократит свои целевые показатели выручки на 2030 год на 14% в день рынков капитала, запланированный на 26–27 ноября.

Днем ранее BofA Securities уже понизила рейтинг акций с «Покупать» до «Нейтрального», одновременно снизив целевую цену до 900 евро с 1300 евро. В результате двух перемещений акции покидают акции с общим якорем стоимостью 900 евро от домов, которые прибыли туда разными путями — один через сброс оценки, другой через снижение рейтинга.

Предостережение брокера обосновано на фоне действительно активной торговли. Rheinmetall сообщила, что выручка за первые девять месяцев 2026 года составила 8,38 млрд евро, что на 38% больше, чем в прошлом году. Прибыль операционной группы за тот же период достигла 1,34 млрд евро при операционной рентабельности 16,0%.

Однако на прошлой неделе компания сократила годовое планирование. Теперь Rheinmetall ожидает выручку примерно в 13,2 млрд евро в 2026 году по сравнению с предыдущим диапазоном в 13,7–14,2 млрд евро. Прогноз операционной рентабельности также был снижен примерно до 18,5% с примерно 19%.

Руководство объяснило внесение изменений задержками в реализации проекта «Арминиус» — программы Бундесвера — и замедлением приемки партий артиллерийских боеприпасов. Эта напряженность знакома инвесторам в оборонную промышленность: компания может расти стремительными темпами, но при этом не соответствовать своему собственному плану.

sum: Two of Europe's most closely watched defence analysts have converged on the same €900 price target for Rheinmetall, days after the German arms maker trimmed its full-year outlook for the second time in quick succession. Bank of America moved first on Monday, stripping the stock of its "Buy" rating and cutting its target from €1,300 to €900. Berenberg followed on Tuesday, reducing its own target from €1,020 to €900 while keeping a "Hold" rating in place.
The Düsseldorf-based group's shares slipped 6.3% on Monday, with a further 0.5% decline the following session.

Bank of America's downgrade rests on softer-than-expected growth in armoured vehicles and artillery ammunition. The analysts also flagged pricing risks, delays on the Arminius project, and slower customer sign-offs on artillery orders. Berenberg's George McWhirter pointed to execution risk and the predictability of medium-term demand, adding that he had anticipated a downward revision to the company's 2030 revenue target at its capital markets day.

Those concerns were validated last week when Rheinmetall lowered its 2026 revenue guidance to around €13.2 billion, down from a prior range of €13.7–14.2 billion. The operating margin forecast was trimmed to roughly 18.5% from about 19%. Management attributed both cuts to the Bundeswehr's Arminius programme slipping into the following year and to delays in artillery ammunition acceptances.

The revised targets sit against a backdrop of robust top-line growth. For the first nine months of 2026, Rheinmetall posted group revenue of €8.38 billion, a 38% increase year on year. Operating profit exceeded €1.3 billion, and the operating margin climbed to 16.0% from 13.1% in the comparable period.

Cash generation tells a different story. Operating free cash flow for the nine-month stretch came in at minus €1,698 million — a figure that underscores how far the company remains from converting its order book into liquidity.

On the same Monday as the downgrade, Rheinmetall announced a Belgian order for 20 Skyranger 30 air-defence systems plus associated logistics. The contract carries a value in the mid-three-digit million-euro range, with deliveries scheduled to begin at the end of 2028.

sum: Rheinmetall shares edged 1.0% higher in pre-market trading today, a modest show of resilience in the face of a week that has seen the defence contractor's annual guidance trimmed and its valuation marks recalibrated by some of Europe's most closely watched research houses.

Bank of America Securities moved first on Monday, stripping its "Buy" rating down to "Neutral" and slashing its price target to 900 EUR from 1.300 EUR. The US bank pointed to softer-than-expected growth in armoured vehicles and artillery as the core of its downgrade. Berenberg followed yesterday, keeping its "Hold" rating intact while cutting its own target from 1.020 to 900 EUR. Analyst George McWhirter flagged implementation risks and the predictability of demand as the sticking points, and added a forward-looking wager: he expects Rheinmetall to reduce its 2030 revenue target by 14% at its capital markets day on 26 November.

Not every house is retreating. MWB Research went the other way on Monday, upgrading the stock from "Halten" to "Kaufen" while holding its 1.050 EUR target steady. In MWB's view, much of the bad news had already been discounted into the price following the guidance cut.

The analyst actions trace back to a profit warning issued roughly a week ago. Rheinmetall now expects 2026 revenue of around 13.2 billion EUR, down from its previous range of 13.7–14.2 billion EUR. The operating margin is forecast at roughly 18.5%, against an earlier expectation of about 19%.

Management attributed the revision to anticipated delays in the awarding of the Boxer project Arminius and in acceptance schedules for artillery ammunition. Revenue from the postponed munitions deliveries will slip into 2027 and beyond, the company said.

The scale of the business awaiting conversion remains substantial. Rheinmetall reported an order backlog of 78.0 billion EUR at the end of September. Revenue for the first nine months of 2026 reached 8.4 billion EUR, with operating profit of 1.34 billion EUR — an operating margin of 16.0%.
The tension running through this week's research notes is straightforward: a €78 billion order book is only as valuable as the speed at which it can be turned into revenue.

sum: Rheinmetall shares climbed 2.8% on Tuesday, catching the broader market's rebound as oil prices retreated and equities steadied after their recent low. But the bounce does little to answer the question that has hung over the defence group since it trimmed its annual outlook roughly a week ago: can the order book be converted into revenue on schedule?

That question now shares the stage with a political one. The Left party (Die Linke) proposed a windfall tax on defence companies on Monday, a move that would hit Rheinmetall's bottom line should the Bundestag adopt it. Two very different clocks are therefore ticking — one set by contract timing, the other by the legislative calendar.

Rheinmetall now guides to revenue of around EUR 13.2 billion for the year, down from a prior range of EUR 13.7 to 14.2 billion. Management pointed to likely delays in the awarding of the Arminius variant of the Boxer project and in lot acceptances for artillery ammunition. The operating margin target was trimmed to around 18.5% from roughly 19%.

Those revised figures are the yardstick. If the company can absorb the Arminius and ammunition slippage within the new plan, the guidance looks sturdy. Any further deferrals would put fresh pressure on expectations. Reliable revenue recognition would be especially valuable if Rheinmetall simultaneously delivers the adjusted margin — growth on its own carries less weight when it comes with added earnings strain.

The reported figures for the first nine months of 2026 give the optimistic scenario its foundation. Group revenue reached EUR 8.4 billion, up 38% year on year, a markedly larger business volume. Operating profit advanced 69% to EUR 1,339 million, showing that growth translated into a powerful earnings improvement during the period. Holding that link intact through the delays is the key test.
A Belgian order for 20 Skyranger 30 systems, valued in the mid-hundreds of millions of euros, adds to the picture. Such wins matter most if they flow reliably into the business plan.
Berenberg cut its price target to EUR 900 from EUR 1,020 on Tuesday while keeping a Hold rating. Analyst George McWhirter flagged execution risks and limited medium-term demand visibility.

sum: Armin Papperger has put his own money behind Rheinmetall for a second straight session, buying stock worth a combined €702,780 across Thursday and Friday. The chief executive picked up shares valued at €502,484.40 on XETRA on Thursday at an aggregate price of €858.9477 apiece, then followed with a €200,295.60 purchase on Tradegate on Friday at €804.40 per share. Both transactions were disclosed in mandatory filings published Friday.

The buying came after Rheinmetall published nine-month figures for 2026 on Thursday. Revenue for the period reached €8.38 billion, with operating profit of €1.34 billion — an operating margin of 16.0%. The order backlog stood at €78.0 billion as of September 30, though operating free cash flow was negative at minus €1.7 billion.

On Wednesday the company cut its full-year 2026 revenue forecast to around €13.2 billion, down from a previous range of €13.7–14.2 billion, and trimmed the expected operating margin to roughly 18.5% from about 19%. Management pointed to the likely postponement of the Arminius Boxer order and later lot acceptances for artillery ammunition, with the associated revenue and advance payments sliding into 2027. The revised figures were confirmed alongside Thursday's results.
The stock fell 1.4% to €818.00 on Friday, extending a sharp decline reported by Reuters on Thursday following the second guidance reduction in three months.

Bernstein Research downgraded Rheinmetall from "Outperform" to "Market-Perform" on Friday, cutting its price target to €1,000 from €1,200, according to dpa-AFX. JPMorgan had already lowered its target to €1,150 from €1,350 on Thursday while keeping a "Neutral" rating and maintaining its warning flag for potential negative share-price drivers.

Analyst David Perry at JPMorgan highlighted the fifth revenue or profit warning in eleven months and voiced doubts about the company's long-term sales ambitions, dpa-AFX reported. Rheinmetall is due to give further detail on its 2027 targets and medium-term plans at a capital markets day on November 27.
Separately, Rheinmetall said on October 30 that the first Caracal vehicles from series production had been handed over to the German and Dutch armed forces.

sum: Leonardo has raised its order-intake guidance for 2026 to roughly EUR 29.5 billion from a previous EUR 28.2 billion — but left every other financial target untouched. That selective upgrade, combined with a weak session across European defence names, sent the Italian group's shares down 3.6%, with Reuters tracing the sector pressure to cut guidance at Rheinmetall.

The distinction matters for anyone tracking the stock. A bigger order pipeline strengthens the long-term business base; it does not by itself lift near-term revenue or profit forecasts. Leonardo still expects sales of EUR 22.1 billion and EBITA of EUR 2.21 billion for the year. Because the downgrade in sentiment came from the wider sector as much as from Leonardo's own release, the share-price move cannot be read purely as a verdict on the company's results.

The figures published yesterday show an operation running well ahead of the pace implied by those unchanged targets. Revenue for the first nine months of 2026 climbed 14.2% to EUR 15.3 billion, according to Reuters. Adjusted net profit jumped 74.2% to EUR 812 million, a far sharper advance than the top line.

New orders reached EUR 23.3 billion in the period, pushing the order backlog to EUR 60.4 billion. Even stripping out the contribution from Iveco Defence Vehicles, the picture holds: ANSA reported that orders grew 22.4% on a like-for-like basis, while EBITA rose 29.2%.

CEO Lorenzo Mariani pointed to the record backlog and improved delivery capability as the foundation for more ambitious objectives in the industrial plan due in March. He also defended the deliberately narrow scope of the order guidance increase.

For all the strength on the order side, the metric that will decide the investment case is free operating cash flow. It stood at minus EUR 68 million for the nine months, against a full-year target of EUR 1.37 billion that management has kept in place. That gap loads unusual weight onto the final quarter.

A timing effect complicates the reading of recent inflows. Alessandro Pozzi, an analyst at Mediobanca, noted that cash flow in the third quarter received a EUR 135 million boost from dividends, mainly from MBDA, which arrived later than originally expected.

sum: Rheinmetall investors got a lesson in reading verbs this week. A framework order may arrive later than planned, while other hardware is already in soldiers' hands — and a fresh sensor partnership sits somewhere in between.

Reports published Monday suggest the Bundeswehr's firm order for Boxer wheeled vehicles under the Arminius programme may not land until February 2027, having previously been expected in early December 2026. The figure attached to that planned firm order is slightly more than EUR 20 billion including VAT — a projected procurement volume, not revenue Rheinmetall has already booked. At sums of that size, the distinction between an expectation and a signed contract carries real weight.

A possible delay shifts the timing of the order; it does not amount to a confirmed cancellation, nor to a guaranteed signature. Anyone weighing the news should linger on the word "could" — the later date is a possibility, not a decision. Shares in the defence group traded 2.1% lower on the day, though the move alone offers no clear explanation of its cause.

The larger point is the distance between procurement intent and actual execution. The size of an announced project matters less than the stage it has reached. A planned firm order and a vehicle delivered to the armed forces are not equivalent evidence of business success.

On Friday, Rheinmetall reported delivery of the first series-production Caracal vehicles to the German and Dutch armed forces. Under the company's own account, the contract also covers 20 years of support across the full lifecycle.

So alongside the possible wait on Arminius stands a completed step on Caracal. The two announcements describe separate projects and should not be netted against each other: the Caracal handover confirms no Boxer timetable, and the possible Boxer slippage does not diminish the value of a delivery that has actually happened. What stands out is the pairing of vehicle and long-term support — the Caracal contract explicitly extends beyond the handover, so the agreed scope of services after delivery matters as much as the moment of transfer.
Also on Friday, Rheinmetall Air Defence and Silvus Technologies agreed to integrate passive high-frequency sensors into the Skynex and Skymaster systems.

sum: Rheinmetall has packed the days before its third-quarter report with dealmaking, and the flurry gives investors a useful counterweight to the one item that has been weighing on the stock: the timing of a major Bundeswehr order.

Shares in the German defence group fell 3.2% as the market digested a report that Berlin may not sign off on a large Boxer vehicle contract until February 2027. As recently as the summer, the award had been expected around early December 2026. The contract's value could also come in below earlier guidance from CEO Armin Papperger, according to Hartpunkt. Neither the delay nor a smaller volume has been confirmed as contract terms.

That single uncertainty has dominated the run-up to the quarterly release, scheduled for 5 November at 14:00. Yet the company has spent the same stretch broadening its industrial and product base, from passive radar sensors to a Romanian shipyard.

On Friday, Rheinmetall and Silvus Technologies agreed to integrate passive RF sensors into air-defence systems. The sensors are designed to detect threats without emitting their own signal, and they will be folded into the Skynex air-defence system and the Skymaster command platform. Rheinmetall described the pact as a step toward stronger airspace security; it did not claim the integration is complete.

The group also said it will present its naval portfolio at Euronaval, running 3–6 November. The lineup includes the Kraken K3 unmanned surface drone, the Millennium Gun naval cannon and the MASS Nova decoy system.

In the naval business, Rheinmetall and MSC won the auction for Romania's Mangalia shipyard on 19 October, paying a joint purchase price of around EUR 138 million. Rheinmetall intends to use the yard, among other things, to build four naval vessels ordered by the Romanian government.

Manufacturing capacity is expanding on land as well. On 22 October Rheinmetall opened the UK Gun Hall in Telford, which at full utilisation can turn out up to 245 barrels and more than 50 breech mechanisms a year.

sum: Rheinmetall investors are being asked to weigh a pair of fresh contract wins and a confirmed bullish rating against a more sobering signal from Deutsche Bank Research, all while awaiting the company's third-quarter figures due November 5, 2026.

Jefferies kept Rheinmetall at "Buy" and reiterated its EUR 1,350 price target, with analyst Chloe Lemarie pointing to the weapons and ammunition business as the basis for expecting a solid quarter. That endorsement, however, is a forecast rather than a reported result — a distinction that matters given the stock's 2.2% decline on the day. A friendly analyst note, it seems, was not enough to lift the shares.

Deutsche Bank Research moved in a different direction on October 27, trimming its target to EUR 1,650 from EUR 1,800 while maintaining its "Buy" rating, according to media reports. Analyst Christoph Laskawi framed the cut around an expectations dilemma ahead of the company's capital markets day: a possible adjustment to the 2030 targets could weigh on earnings estimates, and it remains unclear whether firm order contributions will be sufficient to underpin those goals. The note was explicitly tied to potential target revisions and their knock-on effect on expectations.

On the business front, Rheinmetall has not been short of concrete news. A Schakal wheeled armored vehicle order placed with the ARTEC joint venture — a 50-50 partnership between Rheinmetall and KNDS Deutschland — covers 35 vehicles for Germany and 34 for the Netherlands. Rheinmetall values its share of the contract at a mid-three-digit million-euro amount, with deliveries scheduled between May 2032 and November 2033. That timeline underscores the long-range nature of the business opportunity rather than offering any read-through on the imminent quarterly report — a distinction investors would do well to keep in mind.

A separate agreement announced Friday fits the same pattern. Rheinmetall Air Defence struck a deal with Silvus Technologies to supply and integrate passive high-frequency sensors into the Skynex and Skymaster air-defence systems. It marks a tangible technical upgrade to both platforms, though no quantified earnings contribution can be derived from it.

sum: RBC Capital Markets waded into the Rheinmetall debate on Tuesday with a fresh "Outperform" rating and a €1,600 price target, even as the defense contractor grapples with a reduced sales forecast and a deepening cash outflow. Analyst Colin Moody's call rests on a bold premise: 35 percent annual EBITA growth through 2030, fueled by Europe's rearmament push.

The timing is telling. RBC's endorsement lands days after Rheinmetall published its final second-quarter figures, which showcased explosive growth alongside a notable blemish — the loss of the F126 frigate program. Revenue for the quarter surged 69 percent to €3.289 billion, while operating profit jumped 115 percent to €562 million, lifting the operating margin to 17.1 percent. Those numbers tell a story of a company firing on all cylinders.

Yet the headline growth masks a more complicated picture. Rheinmetall has trimmed its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of €13.7 billion to €14.2 billion, down from an earlier €14.0 billion to €14.5 billion, citing the F126 cancellation. Management has held firm on its roughly 19 percent operating margin target — a signal that profitability, rather than top-line scale, remains the priority. The half-year figures tell a similar tale: revenue climbed 39 percent to €5.227 billion, with operating profit up 74 percent to €786 million and a margin of 15.0 percent.

The market's reaction has been muted at best. Shares were trading at €1,138.60 on Tuesday, down 0.52 percent on the day, and roughly 21.6 percent below their 200-day moving average. The stock sits 43.05 percent beneath its 52-week high of €2,007.00, reached on October 3, 2025 — though it has clawed back 15.86 percent over the past 30 days.

The most striking figure in the half-year report isn't revenue growth — it's the operating free cash flow, which plunged to minus €1.616 billion from minus €631 million a year earlier. Management attributes the outflow to inventory buildup for capacity expansion and timing shifts in customer prepayments. That explanation hasn't fully reassured investors, and it explains why analyst sentiment remains split even as ratings skew positive.

Ukraine’s Armed Forces have shown footage of what appears to be one of the first Skyranger 35 short-range air defense systems mounted on a Leopard 1 tank chassis to reach Ukrainian units.

GAU, an account that tracks German military assistance to Ukraine, identified the unit in the footage as Ukraine’s 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment, part of the Ground Forces. The account said the regiment appears to have taken delivery of the first Leopard 1-based Skyranger 35 systems built by Rheinmetall.

Rheinmetall announced the contract for the systems in October 2025, saying an unnamed European Union country would finance the deal using proceeds from frozen Russian assets under the EU’s Windfall Profit Mechanism. The company put the order’s value in the hundreds of millions of euros and said production and integration would take place at Rheinmetall Italia’s headquarters in Rome. Ukraine had already fielded earlier Skyranger 35 systems mounted on truck chassis; the Leopard 1 version is a separate, tracked variant.

The Skyranger 35 is built around a KDG 35/1000 revolver cannon firing 35x228mm ammunition at a rate of 1,000 rounds per minute, with an effective range up to 4,000 meters (2.5 miles). The system fires airburst rounds that detonate near a target and scatter tungsten sub-projectiles, a design intended to improve hit probability against small, fast-moving threats such as Shahed-type drones and FPVs. Rheinmetall has said the turret shares a high degree of commonality with the company’s Oerlikon Revolver Gun Mk 3 and could eventually be fitted with guided missiles.

Rheinmetall first showed the Leopard 1-based Skyranger 35 publicly in September 2024, at a demonstration event at the Erprobungszentrum Ochsenboden test site in Switzerland. June 24 (Reuters) - Germany scrapped a landmark frigate programme on Wednesday following delays and expected cost overruns, sending shares in the country's top defence firm Rheinmetall — which was tipped to win the contract — sharply lower.

Plans to build six F126 frigates had been mired in trouble for a while, with Berlin weighing whether to hand the contract to Rheinmetall's NVL division after initial supplier, Dutch group Damen Schelde Naval Shipbuilding, failed to meet timelines and budgets.

Germany's defence ministry said it would terminate the programme, warning it would have pushed the cost of six ships to more than €18 billion ($20 billion), up from an initial estimate of about €10 billion.
Instead, Berlin will switch to eight smaller Meko A-200 frigates from Thyssenkrupp's marine unit TKMS at an expected €11.6 billion, partly confirming earlier plans.

"Great news, definitely for us," TKMS CEO Oliver Burkhard said in a video post on LinkedIn, leaving open the option of including industrial partners that lost out on the F126 project, without giving details.

sum: The Düsseldorf-based defense contractor has spent the past week stacking up wins on both sides of the Atlantic, yet the share price tells a story of cautious optimism rather than euphoria. Rheinmetall's British subsidiary has been tapped to supply weapons systems for 72 RCH 155 wheeled howitzers destined for the UK Army, a contract valued at just under £1 billion including service support. That news landed on Friday, hot on the heels of a separate American deal that saw American Rheinmetall named prime contractor for the US Army's "Project Sustainment" initiative — an 18-month program awarded through the National Advanced Mobility Consortium that calls for four hybrid-powered autonomous ground vehicles designed to handle company-level supply missions and spare soldiers from hazardous convoy duty.

Tuesday's session captured the mood precisely: the stock closed at €1,202.20, up 1.18 percent on the day, extending a weekly gain to 4.10 percent. That followed Monday's more modest 0.69 percent advance to €1,197.80, when the US robotics order first became public. The trajectory marks a steady recovery from a bruising spring, though the numbers still carry a sobering caveat — the shares remain roughly 40 percent below their 52-week high of €2,007.00, set in early October of last year.

To understand the current resilience, one has to look back at late June, when the stock hit a yearly low of €902.50 on June 25. The trigger was the German defense ministry's announcement that it was halting the F126 frigate project — a decision that sent the shares into a tailspin. What happened next is telling: CEO Armin Papperger, through his ATP Holding vehicle, and supervisory board member Andreas Georgi both stepped in to buy shares at prices around €953. Those insider purchases, disclosed through media reports, now look prescient. The stock has climbed roughly a third from that trough, and the succession of contract announcements — from Romanian business to the British howitzer deal and now the US robotics program — has validated the management team's conviction in the order pipeline.

Back in 2020, Germany was the seventh-largest spender on its military, behind Saudi Arabia, India, and the United Kingdom.

Europe's defense rally just met its first real test: not escalation, but de-escalation. Even a 32-hour ceasefire was enough to make investors question the trade that's dominated markets for three years.

European defense stocks fell sharply on April 10 after Russia and Ukraine agreed to a temporary Orthodox Easter truce, adding fresh momentum to already building optimism around a potential path toward peace.

Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered a ceasefire from Saturday afternoon through Easter Sunday, halting combat operations across all fronts. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky signaled Kyiv would respond "symmetrically," effectively confirming participation in the pause.

While the truce is explicitly temporary and humanitarian in nature, it marked a rare moment of alignment between the two sides and injected a new variable into market thinking: what if this is the start of something bigger? Markets reacted immediately.

Shares in major European defense contractors dropped across the board. Rheinmetall fell around 5% to 6%, Leonardo declined roughly 5%, while Hensoldt, Saab, and BAE Systems also moved lower. Some smaller and more speculative names saw steeper declines, with losses approaching high single digits. At the same time, construction and materials stocks rallied.

Companies tied to infrastructure and rebuilding, including Buzzi, Holcim, and Heidelberg Materials, rose around 4% to 5% as investors rotated into names that could benefit from a post-war reconstruction cycle in Ukraine.

sum: The disconnect between what Rheinmetall is achieving on the factory floor and what its share price is doing on the trading screen has rarely been starker. Even as the Düsseldorf-based defence group hands over cutting-edge combat vehicles to the US Army and inches closer to a landmark German procurement decision, the stock finds itself pinned near levels that suggest deep investor scepticism.

The equity closed Thursday at €1,072.40, having shed 6.8 percent over a seven-day stretch. That puts the year-to-date decline at 31 percent, leaving the shares a full 47 percent adrift of the €2,007.00 peak touched on 3 October last year. Wednesday's session was particularly bruising — Rheinmetall led the DAX losers with a 3.31 percent drop, slipping beneath key moving averages in what traders attributed to profit-taking and technical pressure rather than any single piece of adverse corporate news. Thursday brought no respite, with the stock easing a further 2.1 percent to €1,068.80.

Against this sombre market backdrop, the calendar is pointing toward a potentially transformative moment. The Bundestag is scheduled to take up the "Arminius" programme on 9 December — a planned mega-order for Boxer wheeled vehicle variants that represents one of the largest procurement initiatives in the Bundeswehr's recent history. Should parliament give its blessing, a fixed contract valued at roughly €12.4 billion could be signed within five to ten days.

The full financial contours of the deal extend well beyond the headline vehicle figure. CEO Armin Papperger has indicated a service agreement worth €4 billion in total, of which Rheinmetall's share would be €2 billion. Two additional options could push the combined framework toward €26 billion — a scale that would meaningfully bolster the group's already formidable order pipeline.

The analyst community is clearly watching this catalyst closely. MWB Research, which had downgraded Rheinmetall from "Hold" to "Sell" as recently as early August — criticising a halved investment ratio and a trimmed backlog target — executed a rapid about-face on Wednesday, lifting the stock back to "Hold" while leaving its price objective unchanged at €1,050.

Rheinmetall's order backlog now stands at more than €80 billion for the first time in its history, fueled by a €5.7 billion Romanian contract for Lynx infantry fighting vehicles and Skyranger air-defense systems. The company booked roughly €11.37 billion in new orders during the second quarter alone.

Investors have taken notice, though the reaction has been measured. The stock climbed 1.38 percent on Tuesday to €1,206.00, building on a 4.08 percent gain the previous session, when shares closed at €1,189.60. That two-day advance follows a seven-day rally of 9.04 percent, suggesting the market is warming to the company's growth trajectory — even as the shares remain deeply underwater for the year.

The momentum isn't just coming from land systems. On Monday, Rheinmetall unveiled the GMF 140, a 140-meter guided missile frigate displacing more than 6,000 tons, designed specifically for NATO requirements. The company has its sights set on a forthcoming North American procurement program, and the vessel's compatibility with the US AEGIS combat system — along with 64 vertical launch cells and modern radar — positions it as a direct challenger to established shipbuilders like TKMS.

The frigate is designed to handle air and missile defense, anti-submarine warfare, and long-range precision strikes simultaneously. It's a bold pivot for a company better known for tanks and ammunition, but one that reflects the broadening scope of European defense spending.

Meanwhile, the land business shows no signs of slowing. The Leonardo Rheinmetall Military Vehicles joint venture with Italy's Leonardo is now fully operational, having delivered its first Lynx vehicles to Italy at the start of the year. The pipeline includes a new Italian main battle tank based on the Panther KF51 platform and additional Lynx tranches. Both partners hold equal stakes in the venture, which is positioned as a central production hub for European land systems.

Rheinmetall is also deepening its footprint in Ukraine. A Leopard 2 and Marder repair hub has been running in western Ukraine since June 2024, and the company now plans four factories on Ukrainian soil.

sum: Düsseldorf-headquartered arms manufacturer Rheinmetall’s Nordic subsidiary demonstrated the latest generation of European mortar systems in a live firing event in Rena, Norway, the company announced Tuesday. The firing centred on the Ragnarok 120 mm mortar integrated into the newly developed Mortar Mission Module.

Weather conditions were adverse on the day, with double-digit sub-zero temperatures and high humidity. The Mortar Mission Module, carrying the mortar system on an HX truck, demonstrated, according to the company, high accuracy and rapid response capability throughout.

According to the company, the Ragnarok Mortar Mission Module provides users with true shoot/scoot capability, allowing them to leave the firing position immediately after the last round is fired. Designed for high flexibility through its platform and barrel independence, the system can be seamlessly integrated into existing and future platforms without significant logistical effort. Rheinmetall says the system is capable of delivering 18 to 20 rounds per minute, completing a four-round fire mission from order to last round in under one minute. Ammunition can reach targets at ranges of up to 8km.

Rheinmetall Norway first showed the Ragnarok 120mm mortar at DSEI in London in 2019, with the dedicated Mortar Mission Module following at the same exhibition in 2025. High-ranking representatives of armed forces, authorities and industry partners from Norway, Sweden, Finland, the Netherlands and Germany watched the integrated system fire for the first time in Rena.

The five nations present in Rena are all active participants in a broader defence build-up, as European NATO countries and Canada are estimated to spend more than $650 billion on defence in 2026, a total that has doubled in eight years. Given their direct involvement in the live firing event and their shared operational needs, these five nations represent the primary potential customers for the newly integrated mortar system.

‘Today’s security environment requires us to act in a targeted manner,’ said Morten Kjorum, CEO of Rheinmetall Nordic. ‘Our goal is clear: we want to deliver systems that meet the operational requirements of European soldiers at the speed that the current situation demands.’

Last month, the company surprised analysts by projecting 50 billion euros ($58.7 billion) in annual sales in 2030, compared with the 9.8 billion euros it logged last year. Its ambitious projections came amid renewed interest in defense spending in Europe and a lack of progress in Ukraine peace efforts.

The Düsseldorf-based company reported a backlog of 64 billion euros at the end of the third quarter of 2025, a fivefold increase from its order book of 12.9 billion euros at the end of 2020. The company stated that the most significant share of its 2030 sales will come from its weapons and ammunition division and its vehicle systems segment, driven by demand in Germany.

The meteoric rise, despite the absence of any major U.S. orders, was driven by increased defense spending in Europe following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. U.S. President Donald Trump has also pushed the EU countries to raise their defense spending goals to cut reliance on Washington, D.C. The European Union unveiled a new “ReArm Europe” strategy earlier this year, earmarking 800 billion euros to boost European defense capabilities, with Rheinmetall expected to be a key beneficiary of the spending increase.

Recent drone sightings in several NATO member states have also raised concerns, underscoring the need for robust air defense systems. Last week, the German firm won a significant order from the Netherlands for its Skyranger 30 air defense systems, valued at triple-digit million euros.

This level of true in-country localization would ensure a strong and sustainable foundation for Romania’s defence industrial base into the future.

Hanwha is scheduled to start constructing a state-of-the-art production facility in Dâmbovița, which will manufacture the K9 Self-Propelled Howitzers (SPHs) for Romania and other land-defence systems including IFVs and unmanned platforms.
